newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak banker says interbank mkt rates too high.
newsitem.headline: Slovak banker says interbank mkt rates too high.

text.p: Slovak interbank borrowing rates, currently between 14 and 15.4 percent, are too high and could create inflationary pressures in the long-term, a leading Slovak banker said on Tuesday.

"Of course we're making money on the market, but in the long-term I see inflationary pressures mounting if the trend continues," Iva Benda, General Director Treasury of Slovenska Sporitelna savings bank, told a capital markets conference.
"I think current rates could force banks to revert to seeking financing from primary funds which could increase interest rates which I already consider high," he added.
Sporitelna, Slovakia's second largest bank, is a lender on the interbank market and the country's largest primary depositor.
Benda said he saw rates staying high until at least the end of the year when the government would enter the market to borrow funds to cover its budget deficit planned at around 25 billion crowns.
He said the move to the primary market would push interest rates up.
"If we seek money from the clients we would have to offer higher interest rates which even now are higher than elsewhere," Benda said.

He said that on one hand banks were under pressure from the central bank (NBS) to lower interest rates nearer to the inflation rate, now at 5.3 percent year-on-year, but at the same time there was outside pressure to keep interbank rates high.
"The NBS is trying to keep banks out of the credit market so they rather go into bills or interbank loans," he said.
